title: AI-Assisted Detection of Postoperative Complications and Automated Clavien-Dindo Classification Using Clinical Routine Data: A Validation Study
summary:
Postoperative complications are a key quality indicator in surgery and an important endpoint in clinical and translational studies. Particularly in liver surgery and liver transplantation, complications are common and have a significant impact on postoperative course and prognosis. The Clavien-Dindo classification is the most widely used international method for the standardized assessment and grading of surgical complications (Dindo D, Demartines N, Clavien PA. Ann Surg 2004;240:205–213; Clavien PA et al. Ann Surg 2009;250:187–196). It categorizes complications according to the therapy required into grades I to V.

To date, the assessment and classification of complications have largely relied on manual review of patient records, particularly discharge letters, laboratory values, radiological reports, and endoscopy reports. This approach is highly time-consuming and resource-intensive and is subject to interindividual variability in clinical assessment. Consequently, the feasibility of large-scale retrospective analyses and continuous quality assurance is limited. Modern AI-based language models (Large Language Models) are capable of processing unstructured medical free text and therefore offer the potential to automatically extract and classify complications from clinical reports and discharge letters. However, whether such a model can reliably detect complications in complex surgical patient populations and correctly grade them according to the Clavien-Dindo classification has not yet been sufficiently investigated.

**Research Question/Rationale:** Can an AI-based language model accurately identify postoperative complications in patients following liver transplantation and liver resection for colorectal liver metastases based on discharge letters, laboratory values, radiological reports, and endoscopy reports, and classify them according to the Clavien-Dindo classification? Furthermore, how closely do the AI-based results agree with the manual classification performed by experienced surgeons?
